---
name: Set up the hunt
description: >-
  Use when the job-hunt story bank is empty, the user says "set me up," or they
  share old resumes: reconcile the resumes, lock the timeline, verify every
  story with them, fill gaps back to their first job, and write their context

---
# Set up the hunt

Builds the job seeker's context file and a story bank holding far more real, verified work stories than any one resume can. Later skills (Score a posting, Build the package) pull only from this bank, so accuracy here matters more than speed.

## Files (shared layout for all job-hunt skills)
- `/home/box/job-hunt/context.md`: contact block, target tracks, location, pace preference, avoid list, a Corrections section, permanent wording rules, and a clearly marked PRIVATE section.
- `/home/box/job-hunt/bank.yaml`: eras, credentials, stories.
- `/home/box/job-hunt/source-resumes/`: every resume they gave you, as the original file plus a `.txt` extracted with a text tool already on the computer.
- `/home/box/job-hunt/render_bank.py`, `bank.html`, `story-bank.pdf`: a readable view of the bank.
- `/home/box/job-hunt/board.csv` and `/home/box/job-hunt/jobs/`: used by the other skills.
Create the folder if missing. Never overwrite an existing bank; back it up (`bank.backup-HHMM.yaml`) and edit in place. Use tools already on the computer; don't install anything.

## Hard rules
- Never invent facts. Every story, number, title, date, and tool comes from the user's words or a document they gave you. Unknown stays unknown.
- Old resumes are leads, not facts. Resumes written by other AI tools often inflate: storage scale, "production" experience with tools only used at home, "led" when they helped, "measured" when it was a guess, facilities or design work they never did, made-up pipelines and metrics. Treat every claim as unconfirmed until the user says yes.
- Always give context when you ask about a claim: which job, which years, and which resume it came from. Never ask about a bare claim.
- Once the user settles something (a date, a title, a correction), record it and never ask again.
- Don't overcorrect. If they correct a claim in one job, don't strip it from every job; ask whether it applies elsewhere.
- Keep private things private. Anything they share that shouldn't reach a recruiter (feelings about a past employer, money, family, sensitive details of a story) goes in the PRIVATE section of `context.md` and never into a resume, cover letter, or shared file.
- Go slow so they think and talk more, not less. Start with one item at a time, then batches of 2, then 3. Go up to 4 or 5 only when they're answering quickly and still giving detail. If answers get short or turn into bare "yes"es, drop back to 2.

## Steps

### 1. Gather and reconcile resumes
1. Ask for every old resume they have, in any version, even ones they think are wrong. More versions surface more stories.
2. Convert each to text and save it in `source-resumes/`. Note what each version targeted (its role and location) in `context.md`.
3. Merge them into a draft era list (company, title, dates) and a draft story list. Note conflicts between versions: dates, titles, numbers, and claims that appear in only one version. Also note how many resume versions mention each story; you'll use that later (see "When is the bank big enough?").

### 2. Lock the timeline first
1. Show the era list with any date or title conflicts and ask them to settle each one.
2. Ask for their official title in each role, and whether what they actually did was bigger than the title. Agree on resume wording that is honest about both (for example "Official Title (workstream lead)") and record it as a wording rule.
3. Mark the timeline LOCKED in `context.md`.

### 3. Draft the bank and show it
1. Write every lead into `bank.yaml` with `confirmed: false`, the source resume, and an `open:` field holding the exact question to ask.
2. Write a small renderer (`render_bank.py`) that groups stories by era, newest first, and shows each story's title, bullet, note, open question (in red), and confirmed status. Turn it into a PDF with a tool already on the computer. If no PDF tool is available, say so in one line and send the HTML or a Word document instead.
3. Send the file as an attachment with a `file://` path, and tell them they can ask to see it any time.

### 4. Verify story by story
Work from the most recent era back, using the small batch sizes from the hard rules. For each claim, ask the questions below that apply, then rewrite the story in their words, set `confirmed: true`, and move on. Re-render the view after each era.
- "This is from [job, years], in [which resume]. Is it accurate?"
- "What did you personally do, and what did the team do?"
- "Did you lead this, own it, or help with it?"
- "Where does that number come from? Did you measure it, read it in a report, or estimate it?" Keep estimates only if they're labeled that way, or drop them.
- "How big was it?" (servers, sites, users, data, events, people) and "How long did it take before and after?"
- "What broke, or what was hard, before you got involved?"
- "Who did you work with on it?" (for context; people's names stay off resumes unless they say otherwise)
- "Which tools did you actually use, and was this at work or at home?"
- "Was there recognition: an award, a promotion, a shout-out?"
Outcomes for each claim:
- Confirmed: rewrite in their words and mark it confirmed.
- Corrected: fix it, and add the correction to Corrections in `context.md` so other skills and later versions never repeat it.
- Doesn't remember: exclude it (`excluded: true`) and keep it off resumes.
- Unsure: put it ON HOLD with a note, and don't confirm it until they bring it back.
- Banned wording: when they say "never write X," add it to the wording rules.
Also ask for new stories in each era: "What are you proudest of in this job that isn't on any resume?" and "Is there a clever fix or idea you came up with here?" Capture the color too (who taught them what, why it mattered) in `note:`, since it helps with interviews.

### 5. Fill the gaps back to the first job
- "What was your very first job in this field, and roughly when?"
- For every gap between eras: "What were you doing between [end] and [start]?"
- For early jobs: title, place, years, how it ended, and one or two stories (first promotion, first big fix, what they learned there that they still use).
- Credentials: certification names, years, scores, any teaching invitations. If they don't remember a cert's exact name, write it generically and never guess the name. Also ask about education and work authorization or clearance eligibility if relevant to their field.
- Side work: homelab, open source, volunteering, community projects. Record the exact scale, and whether it's home or work.

### 6. One open prompt for anything else
Ask once, lightly, and don't push: "Before we move on, is there anything else you can think of that never made it onto a resume? Something you forgot, or something that just came back to you while we talked?" Take whatever comes, ask a follow-up or two if they offer a story, and move on if they say no.

### 7. Targets and preferences
Ask these near the end, once the bank is solid:
- "Which kinds of roles are you going after now?" Record named tracks with short ids.
- "What's your favorite, the one you think you'd be best at?"
- "Are you open to adjacent roles you could do? Anything you won't do?"
- "What kind of work do you want to do more of, and what do you never want to do again?" Record that as an avoid list.
- "Where do you want to work?" Rank cities or areas, ask about remote, hybrid, and relocation, and how far a commute is too far.
- "Do you want a grind job (always on, fast-paced) or a chill one, or should I label each posting so you can choose?"
- "What pay are you aiming for, and what's the lowest you'd take?" Store both in PRIVATE. Use the floor only to score, never in anything shared.
- Dealbreakers, contact block for the resume header (name, city or address, phone, email, LinkedIn), and how resumes should sound (their voice, any taglines they like).
Write all of it to `context.md`.

### 8. Wrap up
Tell them how many stories are confirmed, on hold, and excluded, per era, which eras might still have more to tell, and that the next step is pasting a job (Score a posting).

## When is the bank big enough?
There's no fixed number. A person with one short job may have three real stories, and that's complete; someone with decades of work should have many more. Don't judge by a count. Judge each era by whether new stories have stopped turning up, using two signals borrowed from research methods. Both stay internal: they guide how much you prompt, and are never shown to the person as numbers or targets.

1. **Saturation (from qualitative interview research).** Researchers stop interviewing when new interviews stop producing new themes. Apply it per era: keep a running count of the story prompts you've asked in that era since the last genuinely new story. When 2 or 3 prompts in a row produce nothing new, the era is saturated, so stop prompting it. Expect long, senior, or eventful eras to take more prompts before they saturate, and short or early ones to saturate almost at once. Never keep pressing past saturation to hit a number.
2. **Unseen-story estimate (from ecology's species-count estimators, such as Chao1).** Ecologists estimate how many species they haven't seen yet from how many they've seen only once versus twice. Use it as a rough hint, not a target, and keep it internal: never tell the person an estimated number of missing stories or mention the estimate at all; it only decides whether you keep gently prompting. To compute it: across their old resumes, count stories that appear in only one version (f1) and in exactly two versions (f2). Many one-off stories and few repeats suggest there's more left to find, so keep prompting that era gently. Mostly repeats suggest the resumes have already surfaced most of it. With one resume or none, skip this and rely on saturation alone.

Record each era's status in `context.md` as saturated or still open, without any estimated counts, so a later session knows where more stories might still be.

## Story schema (bank.yaml)
```yaml
eras:
  - id: acme-2022            # company-startyear
    company: Acme
    title: Senior Engineer    # official title; resume wording rules live in context.md
    start: 2022-03
    end: present
    location: "City, ST"
    scope: "Owned X, team of 6"
credentials:
  - name: "Certification (issuer)"   # generic if the exact name is unknown
    year: unknown
    note: ""
stories:
  - id: acme-01               # era prefix + number, never reused
    era: acme-2022
    title: "Short story title"
    situation: "..."
    action: "...what they personally did..."
    result: "..."
    metrics: ["number (measured / estimate, per user)"]   # or []
    skills: [tool-a, tool-b]
    tracks: [track-id]        # which target tracks it supports
    bullet: "One-line resume bullet using only the confirmed facts"
    interview_angle: "How to tell it in an interview"
    note: "Color and context; may hold names, never shown on resumes"
    open: "Question still to ask, or empty"
    source: "interview YYYY-MM-DD"  # or the resume file it came from
    seen_in: 1                # how many old resume versions mention it
    confirmed: false          # true only after the user approves it
    excluded: false           # true for on-hold or forgotten claims
```

name: Score a posting
description: >-
  Use when the user pastes a job URL or job description: score it against their
  story bank and return fit %, matches with story IDs, gaps, and the best track;
  flag any dealbreaker, and only offer to build when none hits.
---
# Score a posting

Reads: `/home/box/job-hunt/context.md` and `/home/box/job-hunt/bank.yaml` (see the Set up the hunt skill for the layout). If the bank is empty, offer to run Set up the hunt instead.

## Steps
1. Fetch the posting (WebFetch, or the browser if the page needs it). Pull out company, title, location and remote policy, comp if listed, must-have requirements, and nice-to-haves. If the page is gone or unreadable, say so and ask them to paste the text. Save the text to the job folder as `posting.md`.
2. Check every dealbreaker in `context.md` (location, comp floor, roles to avoid, required on-site days, and anything else listed).
3. Map each requirement to confirmed stories in the bank. A requirement counts as covered only if a story's action, result, or skills actually show it. Do not stretch.
4. Fit % = weighted coverage: must-haves count double, nice-to-haves once. Round to the nearest 5. State it as a judgment, not a precise measurement.
5. Pick the track from `context.md` that the posting best fits.

## Reply (short)
- If a dealbreaker hits, say so first, name which one and the posting text that triggered it, and do not ask to build. They can still tell you to build it anyway.
- Fit: NN%, and the track.
- 2 to 3 strongest matches, each naming the requirement and the story ID(s) that cover it.
- 2 to 3 gaps: requirements with no story behind it. If they might have an unrecorded story for a gap, ask about it rather than assuming.
- Only when no dealbreaker hits, end by asking whether to build the package. Build only after they say "build it" or "make the package."

Never invent experience to close a gap. A gap stays a gap until the user tells you a real story, which then goes into the bank. Never reveal private context (such as a comp floor) in anything that leaves the chat.

# Build the package

Turns a scored, user-approved job posting into a tailored resume and cover letter built only from the story bank. Works for any person; it assumes nothing beyond what Set up the hunt and Score a posting have recorded.

## When to use
- Build only when the user says "build it" or "make the package" for a posting they've scored. Nothing else counts as a go-ahead, including "apply," "yes," or interest in the job.
- If the posting hasn't been scored, run Score a posting first and wait for one of those two phrases.
- If the bank is empty or has no confirmed stories, run Set up the hunt first. Never build from an empty bank.

## Inputs
- `/home/box/job-hunt/context.md`: contact block for the header, target tracks, voice and tone notes, the Corrections section, wording rules, never-claim list, and the PRIVATE section (read it so you know what to keep out; never use it).
- `/home/box/job-hunt/bank.yaml`: eras, credentials, and stories. Use only stories with `confirmed: true` and not `excluded`.
- The scored posting: `/home/box/job-hunt/jobs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<company>-<role-slug>/posting.md`, plus the score (fit %, track, requirement table, gaps).
- `resume_format` in `context.md`: `pdf`, `docx`, or `both`.

## Sequence
1. **Confirm the go-ahead.** The user said "build it" or "make the package" for a scored posting.
2. **Check the format.** If `resume_format` isn't saved in `context.md`, ask once: "Do you want a Word document, a PDF, or both?" Save the answer as `resume_format` and never ask again.
3. **Select story IDs.** Map the posting's must-haves first, then nice-to-haves, to confirmed stories whose action, result, or skills actually show them. Don't stretch a story to cover something it doesn't show. Order the strongest matches first within each era.
4. **Never invent a fact.** Every line traces to a story ID, an era, a credential, or `context.md`. You may reword to mirror the posting's language; you may not change meaning, upgrade a verb (helped to led, designed to built and delivered), add a number, or add a skill. Apply every wording rule and never-claim item in `context.md`.
5. **Leave gaps as UNKNOWN.** A requirement with no story behind it is recorded as `UNKNOWN` in the record and left off the documents. A fact a line needs but the bank doesn't have (a date, a number, a tool) is `UNKNOWN`: drop that detail or ask the user; never estimate it.
6. **Write `package.yaml`** in the job folder:
```yaml
job: {company, title, url, track, fit, scored_on}
format: pdf | docx | both
header: from context.md (city and state rather than street address unless the user wants it)
summary: {text: "2-3 lines", stories: [ids]}
experience:            # eras in reverse order
  - era: era-id
    bullets:
      - {story: story-id, text: "tailored wording, same facts"}
skills: [only skills appearing in the chosen stories, eras, or context.md]
cover_letter:
  date: "Month D, YYYY"
  recipient_lines: ["Organization", "Team", "Re: Title (req id)"]
  paragraphs:
    - {text: "...", stories: [ids]}
gaps: [{requirement: "...", status: UNKNOWN}]
judgment_calls: ["anything the user should confirm"]
```
7. **Lay out the documents.** One column. No tables, text boxes, or columns for layout. No graphics, icons, photos, or skill bars. Plain section headings (Summary, Experience, Skills, Certifications and Education). Resume at most 1 page for under about 10 years of experience, 2 pages otherwise; cover letter 1 page, addressed to the hiring team, in the user's voice from `context.md`, nothing about pay.
8. **Write the files** in the job folder according to `resume_format`, using a PDF or Word tool already on the computer (for example LibreOffice, pandoc, a headless browser's print-to-PDF, or an installed document library). Don't install anything.
   - Word: `resume.docx` and `cover-letter.docx`, with real heading, paragraph, and list styles, not tables.
   - PDF: `resume.pdf` and `cover-letter.pdf`, from the same content.
   - If no available tool can make a PDF, say so in one line and write the Word documents instead.
9. **Write the record.** `stories-used.md` in the job folder: a short list of which story IDs went into the summary, each era, and each cover letter paragraph, plus the UNKNOWN gaps.
10. **Add a board row.** Append to `/home/box/job-hunt/board.csv` (create with header `date,company,title,url,track,fit,status,folder,notes` if missing), status `ready`. No pay in the notes.

## Check the result
Before returning anything:
- Check the page count with whatever tool is available, and trim weaker bullets if it's over.
- Read the text back out of the files and confirm every claim maps to a story ID in the record.
- Scan for every never-claim item and banned word from `context.md`, people's names from story notes, and anything from the PRIVATE section. None may appear.
- Check verbs against the bank (led vs. helped, designed vs. built, measured vs. estimated) and that any "N years of experience" figure comes from the era dates.
- Check the header matches `context.md` and the dates match the eras exactly.
- List anything you weren't sure about as a judgment call for the user.

## Return
Send the resume and cover letter as file attachments. Do not paste the letter or resume text into the chat. In a few sentences, say the format, the page counts, the main stories used, the UNKNOWN gaps, and any judgment calls to confirm. Then stop.

## Approval line
Building the package is not permission to send it. Never submit an application, fill an application form past review, email a recruiter, or post on LinkedIn or anywhere else unless the user explicitly says to send it.
